introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer FOUR questions in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and two outline maps of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown:
4. (a) Briefly describe the relationship between climate and soils in any one of the following regions:

(i) Northern Lowlands

(ii) South Cameroon Low Plateau. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Climate controls soil formation through temperature and rainfall: they set the rate of **weathering**, the amount of **leaching**, the speed of **decomposition of organic matter** and the type of **vegetation** that supplies humus. A candidate answers on ONE region; both are given here.

**(ii) South Cameroon Low Plateau (equatorial climate; ferralitic soils).**
- *Climate.* Hot all year (about 23 to 26 degrees C, with a small annual range of 2 or 3 degrees) and very wet (about 1,500 to 2,000 mm a year, in two rainy seasons and two dry seasons), with high humidity.
- *Soils.* Deep, red or yellow **ferralitic soils** developed under dense evergreen forest.
- *Relationship.* (1) Heat and abundant moisture cause very rapid chemical weathering, so the weathered layer (regolith) is deep. (2) Heavy rain percolates and **leaches** silica and bases (calcium, potassium, magnesium) out of the topsoil, leaving iron and aluminium oxides, which give the red or yellow colour; the soils are clayey, acid and low in mineral nutrients. (3) High temperature and humidity make organic matter decay at once, so the humus layer is thin and the nutrients are held in the living forest (a closed nutrient cycle) rather than in the soil. (4) When the forest is cleared, the exposed soil is eroded by heavy rain and the iron-rich horizon can harden into laterite. On waterlogged valley floors, **hydromorphic** (waterlogged) soils occur.

**(i) Northern Lowlands (Sudan-Sahel tropical climate; ferruginous tropical and clay soils).**
- *Climate.* Hot, with a larger annual temperature range, and only about 400 to 1,000 mm of rain, falling in a single short rainy season (about May to October) followed by a long dry season.
- *Soils.* Shallow to medium-depth **ferruginous tropical soils** (reddish-brown, sandy-loam, moderate fertility), heavy black **clay soils** (vertisols, called *karal*) and alluvial soils on the flood plains (*yaere*).
- *Relationship.* (1) Low rainfall and a long dry season mean slow weathering and little leaching, so the soils are less leached, richer in bases, but shallow. (2) The sparse savanna and steppe vegetation gives little humus, which is also burnt or eaten, so organic matter is low. (3) Strong evaporation draws iron compounds and salts to the surface, forming crusts and hardpans. (4) Intense, short downpours on bare ground cause sheet and gully erosion; clay soils swell when wet and crack when dry.

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) Briefly show how the prevailing climate in the region chosen above has negatively affected agricultural productivity. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The answer must refer to the same region as in (a).

**South Cameroon Low Plateau (equatorial climate).**
1. **Leaching and erosion.** Heavy rain washes the nutrients out of the thin topsoil and erodes cleared fields, so fertility falls quickly; shifting cultivation is needed and yields drop after two or three years unless fertilizer is used.
2. **Fast organic decomposition** removes humus, so the soil structure is poor.
3. **Pests and diseases.** High humidity and heat favour fungal and insect attacks (for example black pod disease of cocoa, diseases of banana and plantain, rot of tubers and weeds that grow fast), which raises the cost of control and cuts yields.
4. **Drying and storage.** Two rainy seasons and cloudy skies make it difficult to dry cocoa, coffee and grain and to store food, so there are heavy post-harvest losses.
5. **Waterlogging and flooding** of valley floors in the rainy seasons; heavy rain also damages feeder roads, so that farm produce cannot reach the market.
6. **Reduced sunshine** from permanent cloud limits the yield of some crops.

**Northern Lowlands (tropical Sudan-Sahel climate).**
1. **Low and unreliable rainfall.** Droughts and late or early ending of the rains cause crop failure; rainfall is concentrated in about five or six months, so only one crop cycle is possible.
2. **Long dry season** with high evaporation, dry wells and rivers, shortage of water and pasture for livestock, and the need for costly irrigation (cotton, sorghum, millet and rice are exposed).
3. **Soil degradation.** Torrential rains on bare soils cause erosion; strong winds and the Harmattan dust dry and blow away the topsoil; overgrazing and desertification follow.
4. **Floods** on the plains of the Logone in the wet season destroy crops.
5. **Pests** such as locusts and grain-eating birds are favoured by the dry climate.
6. **Shrinking water bodies** such as Lake Chad reduce water for irrigation and fishing.

questions.enonce_markdown: (c) What measures have been put in place by the government to promote mineral exploitation in Cameroon? (7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The government has used legal, institutional, infrastructural and partnership measures:

1. **A legal framework and incentives.** The **Mining Code** (adopted in 2001 and revised in 2016) lays down the rules for prospecting, exploration and exploitation permits and offers incentives to investors such as tax and customs exemptions during the first years and stable conditions for long-term projects.
2. **Institutions.** A ministry in charge of mines (the Ministry of Mines, Industry and Technological Development) supervises the sector; a **mining cadastre** records and allocates permits openly; the state oil company, the **SNH** (National Hydrocarbons Corporation), manages the state's interests in oil and gas; a body such as **MIPROMALO** promotes the use of local materials.
3. **Geological research and mapping** by the state and by foreign partners to identify deposits, so as to attract investors.
4. **Attracting foreign investment and partnerships.** Exploration and exploitation permits are given to national and international companies for deposits such as iron ore (Mbalam and Nabeba on the Congo border), bauxite (Minim-Martap and Ngaoundal), cobalt-nickel-manganese at Nkamouna (near Lomie), rutile (Akonolinga), gold and diamonds in the East, and limestone for cement (Figuil), often through joint ventures with the state.
5. **Infrastructure for mining.** The **Kribi deep-sea port**, railways and roads, and hydroelectric dams (for example Lom Pangar and Memve'ele) are built to carry ore and power the mines.
6. **Regulation of artisanal and small-scale mining** by cooperatives and permits, and training of miners, to bring informal mining into the formal economy.
7. **Transparency and the environment.** Cameroon has taken part in the **Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI)** since the 2000s, and mining companies must carry out environmental impact studies and share some of the revenue with local councils and communities.
